articles.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.summary: The fact the question of European security now features in discussions is viewed in Moscow as a victory, BBC Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg says.
articles.body: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine. That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire. The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace." Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia. What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War. The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin. What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia". That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them. But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow. "In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week. "Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement." The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire". "The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture." Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia. This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US. After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks. But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken. "Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him. And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe. And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield. Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages. But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

articles.title: Dollars Rain From Balcony As Kazakhstan's State Giants Rocked By Corruption Arrests
articles.summary: Days after security services detained the heads of Samruk-Kazyna and state railway KTZ, which control 40 percent of Kazakhstan’s economy, President Toqaev convened an urgent Security Council meeting to reinforce his “Law and Order” drive, address transport governance, and reassure foreign investors.
articles.body: Bundles of greenbacks tumbled from a balcony in an upscale residential complex in the Kazakh capital as two titans of the country's economy were shaken by the arrests of their bosses on corruption charges. The following day, Kazakh President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev called an extraordinary meeting of his Security Council and declared corruption to be the "Achilles heel" of state-owned companies. The events of November 12-13 have made for a busy news cycle in Kazakhstan, even if the details remain murky. There's no clear link between the dollar downpour and the arrests, but more on that later. The people arrested on November 12 are major figures leading two of Kazakhstan's most powerful state-owned institutions. Nurlan Zhakupov is chairman of Samruk-Kazyna, the country's sovereign wealth fund. In its 2021 annual report , the state-owned fund said it controlled "almost all strategic assets" of Kazakhstan's corporate sector, representing nearly 40 percent of GDP. Its total assets reached approximately $87.5 billion at the end of 2025. Yelzhas Otynshiyev is head of Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the state-run rail operator, which has been preparing for an IPO of up to 20 percent of its shares on the London, Hong Kong, and Kazakh stock exchanges, with a potential valuation of up to $5 billion, according to a Samruk-Kazyna press release . Both men were appointed to senior roles during Toqaev's presidency after successful careers in major Western companies. Toqaev described the arrests as "an extremely serious signal of widespread corruption in state-owned companies" and said they should be seen as part of a broader effort to ensure equality before the law following constitutional changes he rammed through earlier this year. Critics have said the changes are more about cementing his grip on power than anything else. They were followed by an election in August , roundly criticized by international observers, in which a new political party dedicated to pushing Toqaev's political agenda won 70 percent of the vote. Speaking on November 13, Toqaev focused on hard-hitting anti-corruption rhetoric. He cited more than 3,100 corruption offenses identified between 2023 and 2025, involving some $560 million, and insisted that no official, regardless of position or connections, should be above the law. "There will, of course, be no distinction between 'our own', 'not quite our own' and, even more so, 'outsiders'. Our constitution enshrines the principle that all citizens are equal before the law. We must uphold this requirement," he said. Founded in 2008 under then-President Nursultan Nazarbayev, Samruk-Kazyna is also central to major state-backed deals with foreign companies and international lenders. Several of its subsidiaries, including uranium producer Kazatomprom, oil giant KazMunayGas, and airline Air Astana, have already been listed on stock exchanges. KTZ's IPO was expected to fund Kazakhstan's railway modernization and expand capacity across the vast country, including along the Trans-Caspian corridor linking China and Europe. It remains unclear whether the listing will go ahead as planned. Rubio Heads To Central Asia As US Seeks Bigger Role In Region Dominated By Russia, China Financial analyst Rasul Rysmambetov told RFE/RL that some potential investors were taking news of the arrests calmly, provided the company's accounts remained reliable. "KTZ's IPO can and should be postponed, though more for financial reasons than reputational ones," Rysmambetov said. "If it turns out this was a bribe rather than money stolen directly from projects, investors will take it fairly neutrally. Those who have already invested in Kazakhstan say: 'The main thing is that the financial reports aren't fabricated.'" Toqaev said some agreements and contracts had recently been reviewed because, in his view, they had been signed erroneously. He gave no details and did not link them to the current investigation. Political analyst Dosym Satpayev says Samruk-Kazyna and much of Kazakhstan's wider quasi-public sector have long operated like a "black box." He argues that replacing executives will not fix the underlying problems. "To paraphrase the plumber from an old joke: It's not just the tap that needs fixing here -- the entire system at the fund needs to be changed!" he wrote, questioning why Samruk-Kazyna had failed to become the kind of state investment institution originally envisioned, modeled on Singapore's Temasek Holdings state-owned global investment firm. Economist Olzhas Khudaibergenov, a former economic adviser to Toqaev, sees the KTZ arrests as an opportunity to confront entrenched corruption. He described the alleged networks inside the railway operator in stark terms: "There are legends that an entire mafia operates there, capable of sabotaging orders and even derailing a passenger train so that an honest manager is dismissed in the scandal that follows." The Horrors Of Aktas Mental Hospital: Inside Kazakhstan's Secretive Asylum He questioned whether detaining three or four executives would be enough to dismantle such networks and whether anyone would be willing to take on the backlash involved in cleaning up the company. The arrests have also reignited debate over whether Samruk-Kazyna should be reformed or broken up. Toqaev has offered no specific plan but has ordered the government and oversight agencies to submit proposals by November 24 to reduce corruption and improve the performance of quasi-public-sector companies. The same day that Kazakhstan's National Security Committee (KNB) announced the arrests, footage began circulating online that appeared to show suitcases and bundles of cash scattered outside the upscale Atlant residential complex in central Astana. The video shows uniformed police officers in high-visibility vests cordoning off the area alongside plainclothes officials. The building is close to the headquarters of both KTZ and Samruk-Kazyna. Authorities have not confirmed whether the incident is connected to the arrests or whether the bank notes are authentic. Some bloggers claimed one of the detained officials lived in the building and that eight suitcases and duffel bags filled with $100 bills had been thrown from a balcony as KNB officers arrived. Local media and online commentators have speculated that the cash amounted to between $15 million and $40 million, though no official figure has been released. The KNB did not respond to an inquiry from RFE/RL about whether the incident was linked to the arrests, how much cash was involved, or what has happened to the money. RFE/RL's Kazakh Service offers informed and accurate reporting in the Kazakh and Russian languages about issues that matter in Kazakhstan, while providing a dynamic platform for audience engagement and the free exchange of news and ideas.

articles.title: North Macedonia: Kriva Palanka seeks help over 1,000 free-roaming cows
articles.summary: More than 1,000 cows are roaming freely through Kriva Palanka in North Macedonia, damaging property and alarming residents. The mayor wants the government to declare a 30-day state of crisis.
articles.body: Recent footage shows cattle wandering through traffic, grazing in public parks and moving between houses , sometimes after dark. Local authorities in the north-eastern municipality of Kriva Palanka say the animals have caused extensive damage to farmland and municipal property , while residents fear unexpected encounters with the large livestock. Mayor Saško Mitovski has asked the government to declare a 30-day state of crisis , warning that the situation has steadily deteriorated. According to the mayor, the number of roaming cattle has risen from around 400 five years ago to more than 1,000 today . Many of the animals previously belonged to a single family , whose members were detained after allegedly obstructing an attempt by the Food and Veterinary Agency to confiscate the cattle. However, the animals were reportedly not placed in adequate shelters following the confiscation and have since continued roaming across the municipality. Residents describe the situation as frightening , saying the cattle appear unexpectedly throughout the town. Municipal officials say they lack the resources and facilities needed to manage such a large herd . Mayor Mitovski hopes a temporary state of crisis would allow local and national authorities to coordinate resources, implement daily measures and find a lasting solution to the problem .

articles.title: France slams Israel’s ‘demagogic’ ban on opposition leader Melenchon
articles.summary: Israel's move came after France banned a prominent Israeli settler from entering the country.
articles.body: Paris has condemned Israel’s “demagogic decision” to bar French opposition figure Jean-Luc Melenchon from entering the country. Late on Thursday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot slammed Israel’s earlier announcement that Melenchon, leader of the France Unbowed party (La France Insoumise), was not welcome. Israel barred the party’s parliamentary group chair Mathilde Panot, alongside Melenchon, due to the “extreme anti-Israel stance” of the party and “outrageous statements” made by its leaders. “This demagogic decision, coming from a government that has repeatedly violated international law, plays into the hands of those who, like La France Insoumise, make a living out of exploiting the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” Barrot, who belongs to the centrist ruling coalition, wrote on social media. “France will continue tirelessly to work toward a two-state solution and peaceful coexistence between the Israeli and Palestinian peoples,” the minister added. Israel accused Melenchon and Panot of making “blood libel” statements against Israel. At the weekend, Melenchon had said that if he was victorious in the upcoming presidential election in April 2027, he would order French ships to escort flotillas taking aid to Gaza. The Israeli military has previously raided such fleets and detained activists. “Israel will respond firmly to those who seek to harm it and will not allow individuals who act against Israel and incite against its citizens to enter the country,” a statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry said. Speaking to French radio, Melenchon said that he had been “banned from entering a territory I did not ask to enter”. The Israeli move came after France barred a prominent Israeli settler last week. Yossi Dagan, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, who heads one of six Israeli regional councils in the occupied West Bank, was denied permission to enter France after landing at Charles de Gaulle International Airport. France’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that Dagan was barred “due to his active role in implementing Israel’s settlement policy,” which violates international law. France was one of several European countries this year to step up restrictions on Israeli settlers, spurring outrage from Israeli officials. Earlier this year, France banned far-right Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are both members of Netanyahu’s cabinet and have encouraged accelerated settlement in the West Bank and pogroms targeting Palestinians.

Russia sends major business delegation to Kabul for business talks with the Taliban
articles.summary: A Russian deputy prime minister led a 70-strong Russian delegation to Afghanistan, pursuing deals on transport, logistics, agriculture, and health products with the Taliban.
articles.body: Russian deputy prime minister Alexei Overchuk was welcomed by a guard of honour when he arrived in Kabul on Thursday with a delegation of 70 Russian business people to conduct business talks with the Taliban government, Afghan officials said.Overchuk met Taliban prime minister Mohammad Hassan Akhund, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs Abdul Ghani Baradar as well as foreign minister Amir Khan Muttaqi.According to a statement by the Afghan government published on X, Abdul Ghani Baradar described to the Russians Afghanistan's potential for economic development and investment, pointing to "strategic location, abundant resources and a workforce of 24 million people".Abdul Ghani Baradar invited Russian companies to invest in agriculture, mining, constructions of roads, railways and factories, and to create a special economic zone in Afghanistan, while expressing his wish to expand exports of Afghan agricultural products to Russia.The deputy prime minister also asked Russia to "provide the necessary facilities for Afghan products to be supplied to Russian markets and to cooperate in reducing transport and transit costs".A Russian news agency quoted Alexei Overchuk as saying that the Russian delegation represent companies that are already operating in Afghanistan and that "many others want to start operating in this country."Overchuk said that the companies represented in the delegation work in the fields of transport, logistics, agriculture and pharmaceuticals and that the Afghan government is interested in Russian chemical fertilisers, as well as in "building fertiliser production plants on Afghan soil".Overchuk estimated that trade between Russia and Afghanistan in the first eight months of 2026 had more than doubled, reaching over 349 million dollars.Russia officially recognised the Taliban government in July 2025, being the only state to have taken such a step since the Taliban seized power in August 2021, after the withdrawal of the United States.Although no country other than Russia has formally recognised the new Afghan regime, the Taliban authorities have so far held high-level talks with many states and have established specific diplomatic and economic relations with some governments.

articles.title: US denies IRGC destroyed American radar in Bahrain after attack on southern Iran
articles.summary: Despite rising military tensions, diplomatic efforts mediated by Qatar and Pakistan are continuing. Tehran has made any resumption of formal negotiations with Washington conditional on its demands being met.
articles.body: The US has rejected claims by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that its forces destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain.US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Friday that the IRGC had launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and that both had been shot down by US forces."There were no injuries or damage," it said.The Guard's aerospace force fighters had reportedly launched a strike in response to an attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik County in southern Iran on Thursday.The IRGC said in a statement that the strike was a "serious warning" to Washington "to put an end to its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz," per the Fars news agency.It added that its forces were on "full alert and ready to respond without geographical limits" should "such violations and acts of aggression" happen again.Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, which plays an important role in maintaining Washington’s naval operations in the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters.CENTCOM said on Wednesday that American forces were continuing to "work around the clock keeping the Strait of Hormuz open for commercial shipping" while also "strictly enforcing the ironclad naval blockade against Iran."According to CENTCOM, around 1.7 billion barrels of crude oil have passed through the strategic strait under US protection since the summer.The latest confrontation comes as US President Donald Trump has taken an increasingly hard line against Iran.Trump said on Thursday that Washington no longer needed an agreement with Iran and asked Vice President JD Vance, who had played a role in diplomatic efforts, to focus on domestic issues at home.Trump also said that Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain had asked him to postpone broader attacks against the country.Despite rising military tensions, diplomatic efforts mediated by Qatar and Pakistan are continuing. Tehran has made any resumption of formal negotiations with Washington conditional on its demands being met, including the lifting of sanctions, an end to the naval blockade of Iranian ports, the release of frozen assets and a halt to the war on all fronts.

articles.title: Russia's Propaganda Machine Deploys Pro-War AI Songs
articles.summary: Russians using streaming music sites might find a new genre turning up in their feeds: AI-generated songs in support of Russia's military and the war in Ukraine. A study by a Ukrainian nonprofit, Terrecon, found nearly 1,000 songs in that category, and researchers say they are meant to generate patriotic sentiment, help mobilize new recruits, and even appeal to children.
articles.body: Russians using streaming music sites might find a new genre turning up in their feeds: AI-generated songs in support of Russia's military and the war in Ukraine. A study by a Ukrainian nonprofit, Terrecon, found nearly 1,000 songs in that category aimed at generating patriotic sentiment.

Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir
articles.summary: Written and smuggled out of prison, the 2023 Nobel Prize laureate's memoir reveals the cost of defying Iran's regime and fighting for freedom.
articles.body: As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes. "A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027. The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW. Mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," says Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over." But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety. In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism . The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection. Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s. In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities. She began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community. In 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani . The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006. Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi . She played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights. Her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life. In her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months. She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care. Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project " White Torture ." "When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely." "This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes. Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these issues to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists. International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all." As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world. Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison. She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats. "We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," says Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it." In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health. Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances. In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons ." But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison. In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban. Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is currently subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?" Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, says Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance."

Appeals Court Lifts House Arrest on Klevi Metaj, Student Symbol of Albania’s Protests, as Police Keep Issuing On-the-Spot Fines
articles.summary: Tirana’s Court of Appeals on Friday lifted the house arrest imposed on Klevi Metaj, the 22-year-old law student who became the face of Albania’s student protests after footage showed him clashing with police officers and later handcuffed to the railings of the Ministry of Education.
articles.body: Tirana’s Court of Appeals on Friday lifted the house arrest imposed on Klevi Metaj, the 22-year-old law student who became the face of Albania’s student protests after footage showed him clashing with police officers and later handcuffed to the railings of the Ministry of Education. The court replaced house arrest with an obligation to report once a month to the relevant authority, according to Metaj’s lawyers. They had appealed the earlier decision of the Tirana court of first instance, which ordered house arrest after he was detained at the Oct. 13 protest . The lawyers said a criminal complaint has also been registered against the police officers involved, over what they describe as degrading and inhuman treatment of Metaj during his detention. Metaj, a University of Tirana student, became widely known on Oct. 13, when students clashed with police outside the Education Ministry. Photos showed him handcuffed to the ministry’s fence, and other images showed him with visible injuries inside a police van. He was taken to a hospital, where he was handcuffed to his bed. The Tirana court then ordered house arrest. On Friday, the Court of Appeals lifted that measure. The ruling comes as police continue to fine protesters on the spot under two emergency acts the government adopted in late October . Since the acts took effect, police have fined protesters 5,000 lek (about €55 or $62) each, mainly for blocking roads or standing peacefully on the boulevard. Partial police figures show more than 65 people fined. Media outlets and civil society groups count more than 100 , and they say the real number is likely higher because not all fines are reported. Unlike Metaj, those fined have not been brought before a judge. Lawyers and rights groups say the fines are imposed at the scene, without a court review or an individual assessment of what each person did. The government’s package also includes measures that give police the right to restrict protests near institutions, remove people from designated “protected zones” and fine participants. Fines can reach 500,000 lek (about €5,500 or $6,200). Last week, student groups asked the Constitutional Court to strike down the acts and to suspend them until it rules on their constitutionality. The protests began on May 31 over a tourism project in the protected Zvernec area on the southern coast. They grew into a broader movement against corruption and the rising cost of living, and in October students clashed with police in Tirana. Protesters are demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

articles.title: Maia Kopaleishvili once again petitioned to be allowed to return to the Constitutional Court hearing, but the judge rejected her request once again
articles.summary: Maia Kopaleishvili, a representative of the Coalition for Change, once again submitted a motion requesting permission to return to the Constitutional Court hearing. Judge Revaz Nadaraia read aloud the grounds for the motion in the courtroom but once again rejected Kopaleishvili’s request.
articles.body: Maia Kopaleishvili, a representative of the Coalition for Change, once again submitted a motion requesting permission to return to the Constitutional Court hearing. Judge Revaz Nadaraia read aloud the grounds for the motion in the courtroom but once again rejected Kopaleishvili’s request. “Maia Kopaleishvili, a representative of the political association Coalition for Change, submitted a motion through the court registry requesting permission to return to the hearing. Constitutional proceedings and the court’s rules of procedure do not provide for a motion to be left unexamined. Otherwise, this motion would have been dismissed without consideration. Since I cannot leave it unexamined, the request is once again denied, given that this matter has already been decided. The court has already ruled on whether Ms. Kopaleishvili should be allowed to return. When a party appoints a representative, and several representatives are present with their responsibilities distributed among them, it is understood that they are expected to protect the interests of those they represent. However, invoking this responsibility cannot serve as grounds for returning to the hearing, because the fact that a representative has duties and obligations to protect their clients’ interests does not give them the right to disrupt courtroom proceedings, show disrespect to the court, or insult it. A party’s duties and responsibilities do not in any way entitle it to disrupt order. In the event of a breach of order, the court acts in accordance with the law. Given that she seriously insulted the court, and considering that she is a former judge of the Constitutional Court, she should understand the significance of the words she addressed to the court. This makes her conduct even more serious, since she is a former judge and should know what it means to tell a judge that they acted on the instructions of the opposing party when making a particular decision. Therefore, this motion is also denied and was not even subject to consideration,” Judge Nadaraia said. For context, on October 11, Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraya ordered the removal of Nika Gvaramia and Maia Kopaleishvili from the hearing. Their removal followed an argument and confrontation between the claimant and respondent parties. Nika Gvaramia had told the claimant party that its conduct was inappropriate. Nadaraia subsequently ordered Gvaramia’s removal, a decision that Maia Kopaleishvili strongly criticized, telling the court that the decision to remove Gvaramia was made on the instructions of Georgian Dream and was a deliberate act. The court deemed Kopaleishvili’s remarks insulting and also ordered her removal from the courtroom. Later that same day, following a motion, Revaz Nadaraia allowed Nika Gvaramia to return to the hearing, but rejected Maia Kopaleishvili’s request to do so.

articles.title: Constitutional Court rejects UNM motion to recuse judge Eva Gotsiridze
articles.summary: The Plenum of Georgia's Constitutional Court has rejected a motion filed by the United National Movement (UNM) seeking the recusal of Judge Eva Gotsiridze. The decision was announced by Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraya.
articles.body: The Plenum of Georgia's Constitutional Court has rejected a motion filed by the United National Movement (UNM) seeking the recusal of Judge Eva Gotsiridze. The decision was announced by Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraya. "The Plenum rejects the motion as unfounded," Nadaraya said. He explained that the main argument raised by the UNM concerned the wording of questions asked by Gotsiridze, which the party claimed suggested that she had already formed an opinion on the case. Nadaraya referred to one of the judge's questions: "Does the party not share responsibility?" He said the question was intended to establish the party's position on whether it accepted any responsibility and did not indicate that the judge had prejudged the case. "The formulation of this question does not express any preconceived opinion or indicate that a position has already been formed," Nadaraya said. He added that the Plenum's members had unanimously concluded that the motion appeared to be an attempt to prevent the judge from asking critical questions necessary for an objective decision. "The court is obliged to ask questions about all the allegations raised and hear the parties' views on them," he said. Nadaraya also stressed that even sharply worded questions did not mean that a judge had already taken a position in favor of either party. Earlier, representatives of the United National Movement asked the Constitutional Court to recuse Gotsiridze from the proceedings. The party's representative, Ana Tsitlidze, said the motion was based on the combination of the judge's comments during the hearing and her reaction to the respondent's answers. "These circumstances give an objective observer reasonable grounds to doubt that the judge has already formed a negative attitude toward the central issue in the dispute," Tsitlidze said. Georgia’s Constitutional Court is continuing to hear a high-stakes lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties, with this week’s proceedings marked by disputes over evidence, procedural rights and the timing of any potential ruling. Tensions inside the courtroom have also escalated, with two leading representatives of the Coalition for Change ordered to leave Wednesday’s hearing. The case, brought by 88 members of the ruling Georgian Dream party, seeks to have five political groups declared unconstitutional and prohibited from operating: United National Movement; Coalition for Change, comprising Gvaramia, Melia, Girchi and Droa; Strong Georgia–Lelo, For the People, For Freedom!; the Federalist Party; and Gakharia Tor Georgia. The petition argues that the parties’ activities threaten Georgia’s constitutional order, independence, and territorial integrity. It also draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission established during the 11th convocation of Parliament. The opposition parties reject the allegations, describing the case as politically motivated and warning that a ban would remove a substantial part of the country’s political opposition. The Constitutional Court began examining the petition on October 21. The case is being heard by a seven-judge plenary panel, and a final ruling is expected by June 2027. The decision will be final and cannot be appealed within Georgia.

articles.title: 09:51 Former Constitutional Chamber judge Klara Sooronkulova runs for president
articles.summary: Klara Sooronkulova, a former judge of the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Kyrgyz Republic, intends to run in the presidential election. The Central Commission for Elections and Referendums of the Kyrgyz Republic (CEC) reported.
articles.body: Klara Sooronkulova, a former judge of the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Kyrgyz Republic, intends to run in the presidential election. The Central Commission for Elections and Referendums of the Kyrgyz Republic (CEC) reported. On November 12, Sooronkulova submitted an application to the CEC to run for the presidency of Kyrgyzstan as an independent candidate. She has become the eleventh contender for the head-of-state position and the only woman among those who have submitted their candidacy applications. From 2010 to 2011, she served as a member of the Central Election Commission, and from 2011 to 2015, she held the position of judge on the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court of Kyrgyzstan. In 2020, she led the political party Reforma, which participated in the parliamentary elections. She also ran in the early presidential election held on January 10, 2021. According to the final data from the CEC, she received 14,005 votes—one percent of the total number of voters who participated in the election. It should be noted that the presidential election in Kyrgyzstan is scheduled for January 27, 2027. Previously, 10 other individuals had announced their intention to run, including the incumbent head of state Sadyr Japarov, former MP Iskhak Masaliev, former head of the Financial Police Syimyk Zhapykeev, former parliament member Baktybek Kalmamatov, and others. According to the CEC, the deadline for submitting candidacy applications is November 12, midnight (00:00). Next, the registration process for those running as candidates will take place.

The information was confirmed to IPN by Violina Moraru, spokesperson for the Prosecutor General’s Office. Present at the court hearing, the suspect told reporters that he admitted his guilt. The accident occurred on November 10, when a woman aged around 30 and a 21-year-old man were struck by a car while legally crossing the street at a pedestrian crossing. The woman died in hospital, while the young man remains in critical condition. The driver fled the scene of the accident but was later detained. According to the General Police Inspectorate, he does not hold a driving licence, and medical tests confirmed the presence of several narcotic substances in his system. The man is also a defendant in a criminal case involving drug trafficking and recruiting minors into criminal activity, which went to trial in 2024.

articles.title: Prosecutor’s Office charges former Penitentiary Service head Giorgi Pataridze and former Gldani prison director Ramaz Pirtskhalava over attack on Davit Peikrishvili
articles.summary: The Prosecutor's Office has charged former head of the Special Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze and former director of Penitentiary Facility No. 8 Ramaz Pirtskhalava in connection with the attack on Davit Peikrishvili, who is linked to criminal circles, inside his prison cell. Pataridze is accused of exceeding his official powers, while Pirtskhalava faces charges of abuse of official powers.
articles.body: The Prosecutor's Office has charged former head of the Special Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze and former director of Penitentiary Facility No. 8 Ramaz Pirtskhalava in connection with the attack on Davit Peikrishvili, who is linked to criminal circles, inside his prison cell. Pataridze is accused of exceeding his official powers, while Pirtskhalava faces charges of abuse of official powers. The announcement was made at a briefing held at the Prosecutor's Office just minutes ago. On October 16, 2026, Vato Kipiani, Shota Kipiani and Avtandil Bilanishvili, who had been arrested in connection with the same criminal case, were transferred to Penitentiary Facility No. 8. Before they were assigned to cells, at Vato Kipiani's request and on the instructions of Giorgi Pataridze, then head of the Special Penitentiary Service, the facility's director, Ramaz Pirtskhalava, decided to place the three men, together with Davit Kacharava, who was also being held at the facility, and convicted prisoner Pavle Gotsiridze, in Davit Peikrishvili's cell. The decision was made in gross violation of the requirements of Georgia's Penitentiary Code and the regulations governing Penitentiary Facility No. 8, the Prosecutor's Office said. On the same day, Vato Kipiani, Shota Kipiani, Avtandil Bilanishvili, Davit Kacharava and Pavle Gotsiridze allegedly physically assaulted Davit Peikrishvili as a group. The violence continued until October 20, 2026. As a result of the assault, Peikrishvili sustained multiple injuries across his body, including four fractured ribs, fractures of the transverse processes of his vertebrae and a concussion. His injuries were classified as less serious bodily harm resulting in a prolonged health disorder. Based on the evidence collected in the criminal investigation, former head of the Special Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze was charged with exceeding his official powers, while former director of Penitentiary Facility No. 8 Ramaz Pirtskhalava was charged with abuse of official powers. Both offenses carry a prison sentence of up to three years. Related Story: Seven charged after Prosecutor’s Office confirms Davit Peikrishvili was beaten at Gldani prison

EU, UK ‘Concerned’ as Kosovo Moves Against Hague Court’s Powers Again
articles.summary: The EU and the UK warn Kosovo MPs not to pass an amended law curbing the powers of the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers war crimes court without consultations with international allies.
articles.body: This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp Protest in Pristina against the verdict convicting four high-profile Kosovo Liberation Army figures , October 1, 2026. Photo: BIRN. The European Union and United Kingdom have warned Kosovo MPs to seek international advice as they review an amended law aimed at curbing the powers of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers on Friday. The legislation was initiated by the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, after the Hague-based war crimes court convicted PDK ex-leader Hashim Thaci and three other wartime Kosovo Liberation Army officials who fought for liberation from Serbia’s oppression, sparking outrage among Kosovo Albanians. The EU Office in Kosovo said that “the amendments raise serious concerns regarding Kosovo’s international obligations and compliance with basic rule of law principles, in particular judicial independence, the protection of victims and witnesses, the continuity of procedural rights, and effective accountability”. In a statement on Facebook, the EU also said that the amendments “also raise concerns regarding their constitutionality”, and stressed “the need for prior consultations before any adoption, in line with Kosovo’s international obligations”. The British Embassy in Pristina echoed these concerns, saying in a statement on Facebook that “we fear that the proposed amendments will do nothing to serve Kosovo’s essential interests and will undermine its relations with international partners and supporters”. The British Embassy encouraged MPs to “take the time for further consultations internally and with the EU and other international allies to find a better solution”. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a hybrid court that is located in The Hague and staffed by internationals but is part of Kosovo’s judiciary. It was established in 2015 to try former Kosovo Liberation Army fighters, under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. The establishment of the Specialist Chambers was initiated in an exchange of letters between Kosovo’s President and the EU, making it an international agreement, and therefore the EU requires consultations for any changes in its legal framework. MPs initially voted for the amended law in a rushed procedure on October 6, under pressure from protests that turned violent outside the parliament building and the need to push through the urgent last-minute election of Kosovo’s new president to avoid the continuation of a political crisis that had lasted almost two years. The vote followed weeks of protests after the four former KLA leaders were convicted of the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder. Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years in prison each and Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi received 18 and 13 years respectively. An appeal is expected. Given the uncertainty over whether the Hague court will indict anyone else, the effect of the proposed legislation is uncertain, however. Kosovo MPs are also undecided on whether the bill in its current form is adequate. On Thursday, at the Parliamentary Commission for Legislation, MP Vigan Qorrolli from ruling party Vetevendosje argued that a redraft is needed. “Our position as the political majority is very clear; we believe that a new legislative initiative – drafted with care and through joint parliamentary participation – would be the most responsible way to address this issue,” Qorrolli said. However, PDK MP Blerta Deliu-Kodra said that, following discussions with other political parties, “we have agreed to pass the bill, but there is no consensus on amending it. We must proceed with the bill as it stands, and subsequently, we will enter the amendment process.”

articles.title: Becirovic met with Macron, discussed the Election of a new High Representative
articles.summary: Denis Bećirović, Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, held talks in Dublin with French President Emmanuel Macron regarding bilateral cooperation, BiH’s European and Euro-Atlantic integration, and security challenges in Europe.
articles.body: Denis Bećirović, Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, held talks in Dublin with French President Emmanuel Macron regarding bilateral cooperation, BiH’s European and Euro-Atlantic integration, and security challenges in Europe. According to a statement from the Presidency of BiH, Bećirović thanked France for its strong support for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He emphasized that consistent respect for international law and the Dayton Peace Agreement serves as the foundation for the long-term stability of both BiH and the region. He specifically thanked France for its support regarding the consistent implementation of the High Representative’s mandate—including the use of the “Bonn powers”—aimed at safeguarding peace, the constitutional order, and the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement. Bećirović pointed out that any new High Representative must be appointed in accordance with established practice; specifically, the decision regarding the selection should be made by the Peace Implementation Council (PIC). He noted that this would preserve the credibility of the international presence and the full capacity of the Office of the High Representative (OHR). He expressed a commitment to further enhancing the friendly relations between the two countries, through the intensification of political dialogue and the strengthening of economic and cultural cooperation.

articles.title: Rosatom set to begin construction of Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant in 2027
articles.summary: Russia’s state corporation Rosatom is set to begin construction of Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant (NPP) on the shores of Lake Balkhash, near the village of Ulken in the Almaty region, in 2027, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy Almassadam Satkaliyev said. «As you know, during the state visit of Russian President Vladimir Putin ...
articles.body: Russia’s state corporation Rosatom is set to begin construction of Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant (NPP) on the shores of Lake Balkhash, near the village of Ulken in the Almaty region, in 2027, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy Almassadam Satkaliyev said. «As you know, during the state visit of Russian President Vladimir Putin to Kazakhstan this spring, Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev announced that construction could begin in 2027… If all the requirements under Kazakhstan’s legislation are met, we understand that Rosatom, together with Kazakhstani partners, namely Kazakhstani companies, could begin construction in 2027. This is the scenario we envisage,» he told reporters on the sidelines of World Atomic Days in Antalya, Turkey. According to him, cooperation between Rosatom, Kazakhstan Nuclear Power Plants (KNPP), the government and the Agency for Atomic Energy has been fairly successful over the past period. «We have already signed an intergovernmental agreement with Russia this year. An EPC contract has also been signed, and fairly constructive negotiations are currently underway on all the necessary annexes. Overall, this lays the groundwork for beginning construction of the nuclear power plant in the near future,» Satkaliyev said. He noted that Rosatom has unique experience in implementing international projects. According to Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev, the state corporation is currently involved in the construction of 28 reactors outside Russia. The first 2.4-gigawatt nuclear power plant is expected to cost $15 billion and is scheduled to be commissioned in 2035. China’s CNNC will build two nuclear power plants of similar capacity. The first of these will be located near the village of Ulken, close to Rosatom’s plant.

articles.title: Billions meant for science misused: SAC audit reveals budget irregularities
articles.summary: Kazakhstan’s Supreme Audit Chamber has reviewed government spending on science, presenting its findings at a meeting of the Kurultai, the nation’s recently inaugurated unicameral parliament, on Nov. 11, 2026. Of 141 completed projects, only 38, or 27%, generated consistent sales over a three-year period.
articles.body: Kazakhstan’s Supreme Audit Chamber has reviewed government spending on science, presenting its findings at a meeting of the Kurultai , the nation’s recently inaugurated unicameral parliament, on Nov. 11, 2026. Of 141 completed projects, only 38, or 27%, generated consistent sales over a three-year period. Another 103 projects, accounting for 22 billion tenge, failed to achieve their planned production or sales targets. The Chamber estimated the total value of financial irregularities and inefficient spending in the sector at 98 billion tenge (about $217 million). Auditors noted that between 2022 and 2025, government funding for science more than doubled, rising from 122 billion to 262 billion tenge. During this period, the National Academy of Sciences was established, universities and research institutions began upgrading their equipment, and new support measures for young scientists were introduced. In 2026, the development of science and innovation was enshrined in the Constitution as a strategic priority. However, science still accounts for just 0.16% of gross domestic product (GDP), well below the 1% target. According to Kursiv.media’s calculations, the gap is approximately sixfold. Meanwhile, the government’s share of total science funding has increased from 55% to 82%. Auditors attributed this trend to weak demand from businesses for research and development (R&D). Between 2021 and 2025, Kazakhstan had four policy documents governing the development of science. Three were discontinued before their scheduled expiration dates, and their targets were subsequently revised downward. For example, the R&D spending target as a share of GDP was initially set at 2% but was later reduced to 0.5%. The planned increase in the number of researchers was cut from 50% to 7%, while the target for private-sector funding was lowered from 50% to 32%. For 2025–2027, the government approved seven priority areas and 153 specific research topics. According to auditors, the list is so broad that almost any research project could qualify as a priority. Project assignments are also often vaguely worded, lacking clearly defined expected outcomes, verification criteria and implementation plans. Of the 393 projects commissioned for 2023–2025, 149, worth a combined 67 billion tenge, were not completed. Auditors also raised concerns about funding arrangements. A total of 62 billion tenge was allocated to 79 projects without detailed expenditure breakdowns. «Even if the final report is rejected, most of the funding remains with the contractor: 96% to 98% of a project’s total value is paid out before the final evaluation,» the Chamber said. Alikhan Smailov , chairman of the Supreme Audit Chamber, said 176 projects worth 16 billion tenge had failed to achieve their intended outcomes. Although monitoring identified these shortcomings, no corrective measures were taken. In 2025, monitoring covered more than 2,000 projects and uncovered violations totaling over 3 billion tenge. However, according to Smailov, the national scientific councils merely «took note of the information» without taking further action. Competitive selection procedures for 2025 projects were delayed by as much as 208 days, disrupting the entire research cycle. The submission of expert assessments to scientific councils was also delayed by up to 93 days. Additionally, recommendations by economic experts to reduce funding for 545 projects by approximately 12 billion tenge were not followed. Auditors also identified potential conflicts of interest among scientific council members. Of the 225 members, 84 participated in research teams working on 127 projects worth a combined 52 billion tenge. Another 27 council members served as scientific supervisors for these projects. According to Smailov, scientific performance is often assessed using formal indicators, including publications, intellectual property documents and records of implementation. However, these indicators do not necessarily demonstrate that a project has produced a tangible technological or industrial result. Projects typically conclude with a final report, but the subsequent use of their findings is not monitored. The audit found that no agreements had been signed for the use of 60 patents included in the sample. Commercialization also remains a challenge. According to the Science Fund, the commercialization rate stands at 44%. However, when calculated on a comparable basis for the reporting year, the figure falls to 16%. The mechanism requiring subsoil users to allocate 1% of their revenue to scientific research has also failed to become an effective funding instrument. Auditors found that compliance with these obligations is poorly monitored and that some of the funds received have been diverted from research activities into bank deposits, securities and repurchase agreements (repos). The audit identified 51 billion tenge in financial irregularities and another 47 billion tenge in inefficient planning and use of funds. Materials concerning 36 violations have been submitted for administrative proceedings, while cases involving three incidents have been referred to law enforcement agencies. The Chamber has also issued recommendations and directives to the government and relevant state agencies.

Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize
articles.summary: Political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran, given prestigious Magnitsky humanitarian award A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.
articles.body: A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”. Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani , an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran . He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night. In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.” He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’” Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK). He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods. His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence. The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption . They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights. Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.” According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners. In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed . In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences. Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.” Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May. Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.” In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”. He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

articles.title: Volunteers from Nine Countries helped Children and the Elderly in Srebrenica, while also learning about the Genocide
articles.summary: Young volunteers from nine countries of the world in Srebrenica showed what teamwork, mutual care and solidarity mean, but also how important it is to learn through experience and contribute to the development of the local community. Through humanitarian work, the volunteers got to know the daily challenges of people living in Srebrenica.
articles.body: Young volunteers from nine countries of the world in Srebrenica showed what teamwork, mutual care and solidarity mean, but also how important it is to learn through experience and contribute to the development of the local community. Through humanitarian work, the volunteers got to know the daily challenges of people living in Srebrenica. Together with the MFS-EMMAUS team, they visited families, helped the elderly, participated in the distribution of meals, socialized with children and preserved the memory of the greatest crime in Europe after the Second World War, Federalna writes. “This is actually a continuation of our summer youth camp, which we have been organizing for more than 20 years here, in Potočari, in Srebrenica, in our capacities. One of the focuses of this winter school is the culture of memory,” explains Sabahudin Mujkić, project coordinator of MFS-EMMAUS. Seyma Akkus from Turkey sees coming to Srebrenica as an opportunity to get to know the history and culture of Bosnia and Herzegovina better, which she had previously learned about. “I read a lot about the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially about Srebrenica, I watched numerous documentaries and decided that I simply had to come here,” says Akkus. However, getting to know Srebrenica did not end at the places of memory. Young volunteers also spent time with children at the day care center in Potočari, participated in creative workshops and helped them in their studies. “I volunteered at a day care center for children in Potočari, where I worked with children. They wrote homework, learned about different new things, and together we participated in creative workshops,” says Ifrah Kutbi, a camp participant from Pakistan. One of the goals of this project is for young people to get to know the other side of life in Srebrenica. The culture of memory remains an important part of the program, but equally important are the people, their needs, and the life that continues here, which is marked by love, not hate. “Of course, it is extremely important to talk about the genocide and the Memorial Center, but we also want to show that there is life after that. We are glad that we have a day care center for children in Potočari, but also that we can provide support to mothers who live in this area, so that they are not forgotten,” Mujkić points out. The volunteers spent seven days in Srebrenica, and they leave with a message to those who have not visited it yet to come, get to know the people, traditions and customs and show solidarity with those who do not want to leave, but to stay and live from their own work in their country.

articles.title: Türkiye, Turkmenistan discuss expanding economic and trade cooperation
articles.summary: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Türkiye and Turkmenistan have discussed ways to expand economic and trade relations during a meeting between the heads of their respective chambers of commerce and industry on the sidelines of COP31, TOBB reported.
articles.body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Türkiye and Turkmenistan have discussed ways to expand economic and trade relations during a meeting between the heads of their respective chambers of commerce and industry on the sidelines of COP31, TOBB reported. The issue was discussed during a meeting between President of the Union of Chambers and Commodity Exchanges of Türkiye (TOBB), Rifat Hisarcıklıoğlu, and President of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Turkmenistan, Mergen Gurdov. The sides discussed bilateral economic and trade relations and explored opportunities for further cooperation, according to the report. Türkiye remains one of Turkmenistan's major trading partners. Bilateral trade reached approximately $2.17 billion in 2025, according to the Turkish Foreign Ministry. Turkish exports to Turkmenistan amounted to $1.31 billion, while imports from Turkmenistan totaled $860 million. The two countries have set a target of increasing annual trade turnover to $5 billion. Turkish companies also play a significant role in Turkmenistan's infrastructure and industrial development. Since Turkmenistan gained independence, Turkish companies have undertaken more than 1,000 projects worth over $54 billion. As of 2025, around 30 Turkish companies were actively operating in the country, with ongoing contracting projects valued at approximately $7.5 billion. Energy cooperation is another major area of bilateral relations. Supplies of Turkmen natural gas to Türkiye via Iran under a swap arrangement began in March 2025.

EU okays consultant team for expert-level talks with Russia — AFP
articles.summary: The delegation will include representatives of the European Commission, the EU Council, Germany, France, Italy, and Poland, as well as the UK
articles.body: LONDON, November 13. /TASS/. EU leaders at Friday's summit in Dublin agreed on a delegation for expert-level talks with Russia that will include representatives of the European Commission, the EU Council, Germany, France, Italy, and Poland, as well as non-EU member United Kingdom, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported, citing a European source. The negotiating team will be the same one that flew to Abu Dhabi this week. Russia, the United States and Ukraine held talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky led the Russian delegation, while Foreign Intelligence Service chief Rustem Umerov headed the Ukrainian delegation. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich and UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan were also present at the negotiating table when the talks began. Despite statements from French officials, no Europeans attended the meeting. Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov said European representatives consulted with the Ukrainian and US sides on the sidelines of the talks. He noted that discussions on whether Russia might meet with the Europeans and what form such a meeting might take would be based on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi talks. Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova pointed out that the Europeans had exposed themselves by holding Coalition of the Willing exercises to rehearse the deployment of foreign military contingents to Ukraine just before the Abu Dhabi talks. She stressed that while the Europeans talk about peace, negotiations and their place at the negotiating table, they are doing exactly the opposite by sustaining, funding and arming the terrorist Kiev regime.

Kallas says Russia’s calls for security talks 'a trap'
articles.summary: The EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy said that allegedly "any kind of discussion about the European security architecture" will only "divert the attention away" from Brussels’ core demand
articles.body: LONDON, November 13. /TASS/. Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, has called on EU countries not to discuss the continent’s security with Russia, saying that Moscow is leading the EU into a "trap." Kallas said upon arrival at an informal EU summit in Dublin on Friday that allegedly "any kind of discussion about the European security architecture" will only "divert the attention away" from Brussels’ core demand - "first a ceasefire," everything else after. She went even further and claimed that the very possibility of negotiations on European security was a "trap that Russia is setting for us," and that the EU should not be duped into doing so. Earlier in Dublin, she confirmed that she is still fully committed to potentially representing the EU in talks with Russia and considers herself, in her own words, a "strong negotiator." Over the past 24 hours, several European officials made harsh public statements in various forms against the very idea of revising the architecture of European security. Head of the European Council Antonio Costa argued that there is no need to reinvent the wheel, European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius said that for security in Europe Russia has to be made "non-aggressive," and head of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen openly refused to answer questions about European security when approaching the media in Dublin. According to the Financial Times, citing officials, behind the scenes, things are much different. Privately, the EU has indicated that it is willing to discuss agreements with Russia limiting the deployment of certain types of missiles, the newspaper says. According to the publication, the Europeans are also open to consultations on restoring conflict prevention mechanisms that existed during the Cold War era. On November 12 in Brussels, at a meeting with representatives of the diplomatic corps of friendly countries of the world majority Russia’s Acting Permanent Representative to the EU Karen Malayan noted that the old architecture of European security, "which has always been associated with NATO, the OSCE and the European Union, based on Euro-Atlantic ambitions, has outlived its usefulness." In a broader context, he warned that the system of colonial domination of the West, which had existed for more than 500 years, had also exhausted itself. Earlier, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that at some point, it will be necessary to talk with Europe about ensuring the security of Russia and Ukraine and the future of the security system in Europe. Moscow has repeatedly declared its readiness to negotiate with European countries a new security architecture on the continent, taking into account the interests of both sides. On October 22, Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed with the US sides' stance that when discussing issues related to "ensuring future security for both Ukraine and Russia, naturally, it will be necessary to talk about the architecture of European security."
